title: Palindromic Substrings
statement:
A substring is a contiguous slice of the string `s`. Count how many substrings of `s` read the same forwards and backwards.

Substrings are counted with multiplicity: two different start and end positions that happen to spell the same text count as two palindromic substrings. For example `"aaa"` contains `"a"` at index 0, `"a"` at index 1, `"a"` at index 2, `"aa"` at 0..1, `"aa"` at 1..2 and `"aaa"` at 0..2, so the answer is 6.

Every character of `s` is a lowercase English letter.

Constraints: `1 <= s.length <= 200`.

constraints: Inputs are JSON-serializable values satisfying the bounds stated above.
hints: Testing every substring against its reverse is O(n^3); instead think about what a palindrome looks like when you start from its middle.
There are 2n - 1 possible centres: one for each character (odd lengths) and one for each gap between neighbouring characters (even lengths).
Walk outwards from each centre while the two characters match, incrementing a counter once per successful step; a mismatch or a boundary ends that centre.

editorial.approach: The brute force enumerates all n(n + 1)/2 substrings (start index, end index) and tests each one with a two-pointer walk from both ends, so it costs O(n^3) time and O(1) extra space. The optimal solution flips the loop: instead of asking which substrings are palindromes, it picks the centre of a palindrome and grows outwards. A palindrome with an odd length is centred on a character, one with an even length is centred on the gap between two characters, so there are exactly 2n - 1 centres (n characters plus n - 1 gaps). While the two characters at distance k from the centre are equal, the slice between them is a new palindrome, so each matching expansion step adds one to the count and a mismatch ends that centre. Every palindromic substring has exactly one centre, so this counts each one exactly once in O(n^2) time.
editorial.why_optimal: The answer itself can be quadratic (a string of 200 identical characters has 20100 palindromic substrings), and reporting it requires touching each one, so O(n^2) is the natural cost of any solution that counts palindromes by looking at them: with n <= 200 the 2n - 1 centres together expand about n^2 / 2 times, roughly 20,000 steps. Within that model the expansion is optimal, and it needs no table at all, unlike the O(n^2) time and O(n^2) space DP that stores a boolean for every substring. Manacher's algorithm does answer the same question in O(n) by inserting separators and tracking the rightmost palindrome's mirror, but that is a specialised refinement outside the scope of this bound.
editorial.pitfalls: Handling only odd centres silently drops every even-length palindrome, which hides most of the answer on inputs such as "aa". Starting the odd and even loops from the same index without shifting the even centre to (c, c + 1) double counts single characters. Testing palindromes by building substring copies inside the expansion turns the work into O(n^3). The empty string must return 0 and the loops must not run at all for n = 0. Finally, expanding while s[lo] == s[hi] but checking bounds after the comparison indexes out of range, so the bound test must come first.
